extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literature; aspiring poets, critics, and general Spectator readership
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-criticism guidance for composing and evaluating poetry and ballads, emphasizing simplicity, naturalness, moral purpose, and national/historical appropriateness. Draws examples from ancient epic and the old English ballad 'Chevy Chase'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: 'universally tasted and approved by a Multitude' — Human Nature is the same in all reasonable creatures; whatever falls in with it will meet with admirers amongst readers of all qualities and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test works against ordinary audiences (example: Molière read his comedies to his housekeeper and children to predict theatrical success). If a piece pleases plain readers it will generally please more refined readers as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential and inherent Perfection of Simplicity of Thought is superior to the Gothick (artificial/epigrammatic) manner in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity pleases all kinds of palates; it echoes the majestic simplicity of the ancients (Homer, Virgil, Milton). Avoid over-artifice when aiming for broad admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity / Understandable Language
rubrics_metrics.description: 'so far as the Language of their Poems is understood' — understood language allows Homer, Virgil, or Milton to please a plain reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensible diction is essential: if the language of a poem is intelligible, even plain readers can enjoy lofty poets; obscure or unintelligible language defeats universal appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Epigrammatical, Artificial Wit for Popular Delight
rubrics_metrics.description: Epigrammatical Turns and Points of Wit may please a wrong, artificial taste but will not become the delight of the common people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epigrammatic or highly artificial stylistic devices can alienate ordinary readers; if your goal is broad emotional effect, prefer natural expression over cleverness for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Foundation Adapted to Nation (Epic Criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest modern critics lay it down that an Heroick Poem should be founded upon some important Precept of Morality, adapted to the Constitution of the Country in which the Poet writes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor epic subjects in moral/political instruction relevant to the nation's circumstances (examples: Homer grounding his poem on Greek discord to promote union).

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate Persons and Actions That Honour the Country
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic poets should celebrate persons and actions which do honour to their country (Virgil's hero as founder of Rome; Homer's as a prince of Greece).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects (heroes, incidents) that raise the nation's reputation; choosing foreign or ill-suited subjects can be open to derision (example: Valerius Flaccus choosing Golden Fleece).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Natural, Majestick Simplicity and Beautiful Incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: The ballad's 'majestick Simplicity' and 'beautiful Incidents' show a poetical genius guided by nature rather than artificial ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ natural incidents and majestic simplicity of thought/expression to produce effects like those of the ancients; such simplicity can be 'gorgeous' in its own way and move both common and refined readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Let Rustic Simplicity Prejudice Judgment of Thought's Greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution the reader not to let the simplicity of the stile, which one may well pardon in so old a poet, prejudice him against the greatness of the thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple or antiquated 'apparel' should not lead critics to underrate the underlying power of thought; evaluate thought and expression separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evocative, Universal Heroic Gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Small but powerful acts (e.g., 'Taking the dead Man by the Hand') convey heroic compassion and connect to classical exemplars (Aeneas and Lausus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include vivid, humane gestures that evoke universal sympathy and heroic character; such particular actions can create strong emotional resonance and classical echoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoke Posterity / Future Consequences to Heighten Gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines like 'The Child may rue that was unborn' consider misfortunes brought upon posterity; invoking future consequences conforms to the way of the ancient poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referencing long-term or generational consequences adds majesty and moral weight to events and quarrels in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and Rhythm (Sonorous Numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ballad contains sonorous numbers and musical quality; 'the Numbers [sonorous;] ... the Apparel is much more gorgeous than many of the Poets made use of'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to sound and meter; musical, sonorous lines contribute to majesty and public delight even when diction is rustic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Depiction of Transformative Emotion (Love)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refining passions to a greater elegance often happens by the mere force and dignity of the object; Dryden's Cymon example shows a natural transformation that appears 'as Natural as Wonderful'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray transformations (e.g., a clownish character moved by beauty) in vivid, believable detail; authenticity of feeling is persuasive and pleasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and Sincerity in Low/Popular Forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The verbatim love-letter of a country footman exemplifies sincere, confused, rustic expression that can be affecting when presented faithfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine voice—even in humble or unpolished forms—can be valuable literary material; preserving the authentic tone can enhance effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring Admiration Comes from Inward Qualities, Not Mere Appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Lasting admiration is not to be hoped for from Beauty, Dress, or Fashion, but from inward ornaments which are not defaced by time or sickness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating characters or moral lessons, emphasize durable virtues (education, fidelity, care) over transient external charms to win lasting esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Designing for Affected or Ignorant Tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordinary song that delights the common people will please all such readers 'as are not unqualified for the Entertainment by their Affectation or Ignorance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not tailor work to affectation; recognize that some readers' failure to enjoy simple, natural works stems from artificial tastes or ignorance rather than defects in the work.
